item.title: AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training
item.description:
AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training

AWS has released the Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC), a pre-integrated software stack designed to simplify distributed machine learning training. The image is built, tested as a single unit, and maintained by AWS to ensure compatibility across the various libraries required for multi-node workloads.

🔍 Overview

The Ray Train DLC is a PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries layered on top. It includes the full HuggingFace training stack, allowing users to run fine-tuning jobs without building or pushing new images. AWS publishes these images to the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public, where they can be pulled without credentials.

Component Function
CUDA Runtime Provides the foundational environment for GPU acceleration.
PyTorch Compiled against the specific CUDA runtime in the image.
NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library for GPU communication.
EFA Libraries Userspace libraries for the Elastic Fabric Adapter.
AWS OFI NCCL Plugin Connects NCCL to EFA for high-performance networking.
Ray Coordinates the cluster and manages training libraries.

🧩 How it works

Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two distinct roles, both of which use the same tagged image. Whether running on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) via KubeRay or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), the container’s role is determined by the startup command.

  • Ray Head: Coordinates the cluster, tracks state in the global control store, and runs the dashboard and job server.
  • Ray Worker: Supplies GPUs and executes the training processes, connecting to the head’s address at startup.

On Kubernetes, the KubeRay operator adds a RayCluster resource that builds and maintains these groups from a single manifest.

⚙️ Key details

The Ray Train DLC is designed to be configured entirely from outside the image. Users specify instance types, GPU counts, and network transport settings through external configuration files rather than by modifying the container.

  • Compatibility: The image entrypoint automatically enables bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries if the host’s NVIDIA driver is older than the image’s CUDA version.
  • Performance: Collective operations between instances run over EFA automatically as soon as pods request it, as the EFA stack is pre-installed.
  • Testing: AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests.

🚀 Availability

The Ray Train DLC is available in the Amazon ECR repository under the train-ml tag prefix, sharing a repository with Ray Serve and Ray LLM DLCs.

A provided sample demonstrates the DLC’s capabilities by fine-tuning a Qwen2.5-1.5B model using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances.

#AWS #Ray #PyTorch #MachineLearning #Kubernetes

Source: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
item.description:
Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers

This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the multi‑node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers. The deployment separates the prefill and decode phases onto distinct GPU workers behind a single OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.

🔍 Overview

  • Ray is a distributed compute framework; Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) are pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately.
  • The new Ray LLM DLC extends this approach to multi‑node inference.

🏗️ Architecture

  • CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod (CPU‑only).
  • Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run Ray workers: one dedicated to the prefill phase, the other to the decode phase.
  • Both GPU nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
  • KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and automatically wires the head‑to‑worker join.
  • Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers.
  • KV‑cache generated by prefill is transferred to the decode worker over NIXL, using the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) through NIXL’s libfabric backend.

⚙️ How It Works

  • Prefill phase
    • Processes the entire input prompt in parallel.
    • Builds the key‑value (KV) cache.
    • Compute‑bound.
  • Decode phase
    • Generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending the KV cache.
    • Memory‑bandwidth‑bound.
  • Separating the phases prevents compute‑heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress.
  • Disaggregation allows each phase to use hardware and serving properties tuned to its workload, improving overall performance at scale.
  • The trade‑off is that the KV cache must be handed from prefill to decode quickly enough to retain the benefit.

📦 Key Components

Component Role
Ray LLM DLC Packages Ray Serve LLM, NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL), and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack; exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API with no application code
vLLM Inference engine
Ray Serve HTTP Serving layer
NIXL KV‑cache transfer between nodes
EFA stack (libfabric, aws‑ofi‑nccl) High‑bandwidth node‑to‑node communication
AWS Deep Learning Containers Pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images ensuring no version drift between CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer

🚀 Deployment Details

  • The Ray LLM DLC ships Ray Serve LLM, NIXL, and the EFA stack, ready for multi‑node inference.
  • No application code is required to expose the OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.
  • This multi‑node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as for prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads.
  • In a previous post, the Ray Serve DLC was used to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By assigning prefill and decode to separate GPUs, compute‑heavy prefill work no longer contends with latency‑sensitive decode work.
  • Independent scaling of each phase enables better resource utilization and lower latency for LLM serving at scale.
  • All components are validated together before each release, guaranteeing compatibility across the CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer.

#AWS #Ray #LLM #Kubernetes #Inference

Source: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers | Amazon Web Services
